newsitem.title: USA: U.S approval of new drugs compares favorably - study.
newsitem.headline: U.S approval of new drugs compares favorably - study.

text.p: Seeking to dispel criticism that U.S. regulators are slow to approve useful new drugs, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration said on Tuesday a comparative study showed it was faster than Germany and Japan in approving new medicines.
Critics have blamed the FDA for creating a "drug lag" where medicines approved for patients elsewhere have not been available in the United States.

The agency's outgoing commissioner, David Kessler, wrote the study published in the Journal of the American Medical Association comparing the status of 214 drugs that sought approval between 1990 and 1994 in the United States, Britain, Germany and Japan. The four countries accounted for 60 percent of global pharmaceutical sales.

Britain was seen as the most aggressive in approving new therapies, with the United States a close second and Germany and Japan lagging behind. Among the study's findings, the FDA said of 41 drugs approved in three of the four countries, Britain was the first to approve 16 products, the United States 15, Japan six and Germany four.

The FDA focused on approvals of "priority" drugs, defined as offering at least a modest advance compared to existing therapies or providing treatment for a condition where there was no alternate treatment.
"The findings ... clearly support the conclusion that the FDA's standards do not delay consumer access to safe and effective drugs, compared to other countries," Kessler and his colleagues wrote.
"Indeed, this conclusion is a conservative one; in may cases, the U.S. system allows priority drugs to reach consumers before they become more widely available."
In a speech on Tuesday to the Food and Drug Law Institute in Washington, Kessler said American patients were getting the medications they need faster and more efficiently than ever before.

Kessler said in the late 1980s it took an average of 30 months for a new drug to gain U.S. approval, but that the average so far this year was just 15 months. And he said the average approval time for priority drugs, such as those to treat AIDS, was 7.8 months.
